question: Figure shows three circular arcs, each of radius $R$ and total charge as indicated. The net electric potential at the centre of curvature is
solution:
For any circular arc of radius R carrying a total charge q .

Let dq be an infinitesimal element of charge located on the arc.

Since every point on the arc is at a constant distance R from the centre of curvature, the potential dV produced at the centre by the element dq is,

\mathrm{dV}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{\mathrm{dq}}{\mathrm{R}}

So, the total electric potential at centre over the entire arc is;

V=\int d V=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R} \int d q=\frac{q_{\text {net }}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R}

So, the electric potential at the centre of curvature depends only on the net charge on the arc and its radius R , independent of the angle subtended or the distribution of the charge along the arc.

All three separate arcs having the same radius of curvature R.

First arc carries a total charge of $+Q$

Second arc carries a total charge of $-2Q$

Third arc carries a total charge of $+3Q$

Since electric potential is a scalar quantity, the total potential $V_{\text{net}}$ at the common centre of curvature is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to each individual arc.

V_{\text{net}} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3

V_{\text{net}} = +\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} + \left(-\frac{2Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}\right) + \left(+\frac{3Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}\right)

V_{\text{net}} = \frac{Q - 2Q + 3Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}

V_{\text{net}} = \frac{2Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} = \frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R}

Thus, the correct option is (A)

question: A charge is uniformly distributed inside a spherical body of radius $r_1 = 2r_0$ having a concentric cavity of radius $r_2 = r_0$ ($\rho$ is charge density inside the sphere). Potential of a point P at a distance $\frac{3r_0}{2}$ from centre is
solution:
Taking electric potential reference at infinity $(\mathrm{V}(\infty)=0)$, electric potential $\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{r})$ at a radial distance r from the centre is related to the radial electric field $\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{r})$ as,

\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{r})=-\int\limits_{\infty}^{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{E}\left(\mathrmr^{\prime}\right) \mathrm{dr}^{\prime}=\int\limits_{\mathrm{r}}^{\infty} \mathrm{E}\left(\mathrmr^{\prime}\right) \mathrm{dr}^{\prime}

Using Gauss law, the electric field at any distance $r$, is

\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{a} \, = \frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E(r) \cdot 4\pi r^2 = \frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E(r) = \frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}

Here, the charged spherical body has cavity region $0 \leq r < r_0$ where $\rho = 0$.

Charged region is $r_0 \leq r \leq 2r_0$ with uniform charge density $\rho$.

Exterior region is $r > 2r_0$ where $\rho = 0$.

The point P is at distance $r_P = \frac{3r_0}{2}$ from the center, this point lies inside the charged region since $r_0 < \frac{3r_0}{2} < 2r_0$.

V\left(\frac{3r_0}{2}\right) = \int\limits_{\frac{3r_0}{2}}^{r_0} E_{\text{inside}}(r)\,dr + \int\limits_{2r_0}^{\infty} E_{\text{outside}}(r)\,dr

Here, $\int\limits_{2r_0}^{\infty} E_{\text{outside}}(r)\,dr$ is the potential at the outer surface of the spherical shell, $V(2r_0)$.

V(2r_0) = \int\limits_{2r_0}^{\infty} E_{\text{outside}}(r)\,dr

For $r \geq 2r_0$, the total enclosed charge is the entire charge of the hollow sphere.

q_{\text {total }}=\rho \cdot V_{\text {shell }}=\rho\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi\left(2 r_0\right)^3-\frac{4}{3} \pi r_0^3\right)=\frac{4}{3} \pi \rho\left(8 r_0^3-r_0^3\right)=\frac{28}{3} \pi \rho r_0^3

By Gauss's law, for $\mathrm{r} \geq 2 \mathrm{r}_0, \mathrm{E}_{\text {outside }}(\mathrm{r})=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {total }}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{r}^2}$

Therefore, the potential at the outer surface ( $\mathrm{r}=2 \mathrm{r}_0$ ) is,

V\left(2 r_0\right)=\frac{q_{\text {total }}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0\left(2 r_0\right)}=\frac{\frac{28}{3} \pi \rho r_0^3}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0\left(2 r_0\right)}=\frac{28 \rho r_0^2}{24 \varepsilon_0}=\frac{7 \rho r_0^2}{6 \varepsilon_0}

For any radius $r$ such that $r_0 \leq r \leq 2 r_0$, the charge enclosed inside a concentric sphere of radius $r$ is,

q_{\text{enclosed}}(r)=\rho\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3-\frac{4}{3}\pi r_0^3\right)=\frac{4}{3}\pi\rho\left(r^3-r_0^3\right)

Applying Gauss's law,

E_{\text{inside}}(r)\cdot 4\pi r^2=\frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi\rho\left(r^3-r_0^3\right)}{\varepsilon_0}

E_{\text{inside}}(r)=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left(r-\frac{r_0^3}{r^2}\right)

On integrating $E_{\text{inside}}(r)$ from $r=\frac{3r_0}{2}$ to $r=2r_0$.

\Delta V=\int\limits_{\frac{3r_0}{2}}^{2r_0} E_{\text{inside}}(r)\,dr=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\int\limits_{\frac{3r_0}{2}}^{2r_0}\left(r-\frac{r_0^3}{r^2}\right)dr

\Delta V=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{r^2}{2}+\frac{r_0^3}{r}\right]_{\frac{3r_0}{2}}^{2r_0}

\Delta V=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left[\left(\frac{(2r_0)^2}{2}+\frac{r_0^3}{2r_0}\right)-\left(\frac{\left(\frac{3r_0}{2}\right)^2}{2}+\frac{r_0^3}{\left(\frac{3r_0}{2}\right)}\right)\right]

\Delta V=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left[\left(2r_0^2+\frac{1}{2}r_0^2\right)-\left(\frac{9}{8}r_0^2+\frac{2}{3}r_0^2\right)\right]

\Delta V=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left[\left(\frac{5}{2}r_0^2\right)-\left(\frac{43}{24}r_0^2\right)\right]

\Delta V=\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{60-43}{24}\right]r_0^2=\left(\frac{\rho}{3\varepsilon_0}\right)\times \frac{17}{24}r_0^2

\Delta V=\frac{17\rho r_0^2}{72\varepsilon_0}

So, total potential at point P is

V\left(\frac{3r_0}{2}\right)=\Delta V+V(2r_0)

V\left(\frac{3r_0}{2}\right)=\frac{17\rho\, r_0^2}{72\varepsilon_0}+\frac{7\rho\, r_0^2}{6\varepsilon_0}

V\left(\frac{3r_0}{2}\right)=\frac{17\rho\, r_0^2}{72\varepsilon_0}+\frac{84\rho\, r_0^2}{72\varepsilon_0}=\frac{(17+84)\rho\, r_0^2}{72\varepsilon_0}=\frac{101\rho\, r_0^2}{72\varepsilon_0}

Thus, the correct option is (B)

question: Three particles of charge +2Q, −Q and −Q are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle ABC as shown in the figure. Now, a fourth particle of charge +Q is to be moved slowly from the centroid G to the mid-point D of side BC of the triangle. The work done by the external agent in order to move this fourth charge is given by
solution:
When the object is moved slowly then its speed is constant, i.e., change in kinetic energy is zero.

When a charge q is moved from an initial point G to a final point D in an electrostatic field, the work done by the external agent $\mathrm{W}_{\text {ext }}$ is equal to the change in electric potential energy of the system.

\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathrm{q}\left(\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{D}}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{G}}\right)

Here $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{G}}$ is the electric potential at point G due to the three fixed charges, and $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the electric potential at point D due to the three fixed charges. Here, the moving charge is $\mathrm{q}=+\mathrm{Q}$.

Let a be the length of each side of the equilateral triangle ABC.

AB = BC = CA = a

The altitude AD of the equilateral triangle from vertex A to side BC has length

AD = a\sin(60^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a

Since the centroid G divides the median AD in the ratio 2:1, distance of centroid G from vertex A.

r_{GA} = \frac{2}{3}AD = \frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\right) = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}

Using symmetry distance of centroid G from vertex B and vertex C is $r_{GB} = r_{GC} = r_{GA} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}$

Using the superposition principle for potential, the potential at centroid is

V_G = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_A}{r_{GA}} + \frac{q_B}{r_{GB}} + \frac{q_C}{r_{GC}}\right)

Since $r_{GA} = r_{GB} = r_{GC} = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}$,

V_G = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\right)}(q_A + q_B + q_C)

V_G = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\right)}\left[(+2Q) + (-Q) + (-Q)\right] = 0 \Rightarrow V_G = 0

Point D is the midpoint of side BC, so distance from vertex B and C to point D is $r_{DB} = r_{DC} = \frac{a}{2}$ and distance from vertex A to point D is equal to altitude length, $r_{DA} = AD = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$

So, electric potential at point D is

V_D = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{q_A}{r_{DA}} + \frac{q_B}{r_{DB}} + \frac{q_C}{r_{DC}}\right)

V_D = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{(+2Q)}{\sqrt{3}/2a} + \frac{-Q}{a/2} + \frac{(-Q)}{a/2}\right)

V_D = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{4Q}{\sqrt{3}a} - \frac{4Q}{a}\right) = \frac{4Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} - 1\right) = \frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} - 1\right) = -\frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)

Substituting $q = +Q$, $V_D$, and $V_G = 0$ into the work formula,

W_{\mathrm{ext}} = (+Q)(V_D - V_G) = Q\left[-\frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) - 0\right]

W_{\mathrm{ext}} = -\frac{Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)

Thus, the correct option is (B)

solution:
Let the horizontal axis be the x -axis and the vertical axis be the y -axis and point P be chosen as the origin $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{\mathrm{P}}=(0,0)$

The total distance from the line through points A and B to the line through points D, Q, and C is 0.2 m in two grid intervals. Thus, the height of one grid square is \Delta y = \frac{0.2\ \mathrm{m}}{2} = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}

Similarly, the total distance from the bottom line through points A and D is 0.2 m, in two grid intervals. Thus, the width of one grid square is \Delta y = \frac{0.2\ \mathrm{m}}{2} = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}

Using point P as $(0,0)$, the coordinates of the other points are A $= (-0.1\ \mathrm{m}, -0.1\ \mathrm{m})$, B $= (-0.1\ \mathrm{m}, +0.1\ \mathrm{m})$, C $= (+0.1\ \mathrm{m}, +0.1\ \mathrm{m})$, D $= (+0.1\ \mathrm{m}, -0.1\ \mathrm{m})$ and Q $= (+0.1\ \mathrm{m}, 0)$

In a uniform electric field \vec{E} = E_x\,\hat{i} + E_y\,\hat{j}, the relation between the electric field and the electric potential difference between any two points is \Delta V = -\int\limits \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r} = -\vec{E} \cdot \Delta \vec{r}

V(\vec{r}_2) - V(\vec{r}_1) = -\left[E_x(x_2-x_1)+E_y(y_2-y_1)\right]

Between point P$(0,0)$ and point B $(-0.1,+0.1)$,

V(B)-V(P) = -\left[E_x(-0.1-0) + E_y(0.1-0)\right]

The potential of point B is $V(B)=5\ \mathrm{V}$ and that on point P is $V(P)=5\ \mathrm{V}$,

5-5 = 0.1\,E_x - 0.1\,E_y \Rightarrow 0.1(E_x-E_y)=0 \Rightarrow E_x=E_y

Between point P$(0,0)$ and point A$(-0.1,-0.1)$,

V(A)-V(P) = -\left[E_x(-0.1-0) + E_y(-0.1-0)\right] = 0.1\,E_x + 0.1\,E_y

The potential of point A is $V(A)=2\ \mathrm{V}$ and that of point P is $V(P)=5\ \mathrm{V}$,

2-5 = 0.1(E_x+E_y) \Rightarrow -3 = 0.1(E_x+E_y) \Rightarrow E_x+E_y=-30\ \mathrm{V/m}

Since $E_x=E_y \Rightarrow 2E_x=-30 \Rightarrow E_x=-15\ \mathrm{V/m}; E_y=-15\ \mathrm{V/m}$

So, the electric field vector is

\vec{E} = -15\hat{i} - 15\hat{j}\ \mathrm{V/m} = -15(\hat{i}+\hat{j})\ \mathrm{V/m}

The magnitude of $\vec{E}$ is

|\vec{E}| = \sqrt{(-15)^2 + (-15)^2} = \sqrt{225+225} = \sqrt{450} = 15\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V/m}

The direction of the vector connecting point P to point A is

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{\mathrm{PA}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{\mathrm{A}}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{\mathrm{P}}=(-0.1 \hat{\imath}-0.1 \hat{\jmath})-(0)=-0.1(\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}) \mathrm{m}

The unit vector along $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{\mathrm{PA}}$ is $\hat{\mathrm{u}}_{\mathrm{PA}}=\frac{-0.1 \hat{\imath}-0.1 \hat{\jmath}}{\sqrt{(-0.1)^2+(-0.1)^2}}=\frac{-\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}}{\sqrt{2}}$

The unit vector of the electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is $\hat{\mathrm{u}}_{\mathrm{E}}=\frac{-15 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-15 \hat{\mathrm{j}}}{15 \sqrt{2}}=\frac{-\hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}$

Since $\hat{\mathrm{u}}_{\mathrm{E}}=\hat{\mathrm{u}}_{\mathrm{PA}}$, the electric field points along the vector from P to A (along PA).

Therefore $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=15 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{Vm}^{-1}$ along PA. Thus, the correct option is (B).

question: A point charge q is placed at the corner of an equilateral prism. Then, the electric flux through the prism is
solution:
An equilateral prism has a triangular cross-section whose interior angles are each 60°.

A corner of the prism is the intersection of three planes, the triangular end face and two rectangular side faces.

Around a single line passing through a point, a full rotation in a plane is $360^{\circ}$.

Since the corner angle of the equilateral triangle is $60^{\circ}$, number of prisms around the vertical edge is,

N=\frac{360^{\circ}}{60^{\circ}}=6

Placing 6 such prisms around the common vertical edge forms a regular hexagonal prism that covers the entire 360° around the vertical edge, but only on one side of the base plane.

The charge is at the corner, so it lies on the boundary plane of the base.

To enclose the remaining space on the other side of this plane, an identical arrangement of 6 prisms must be placed left the first set.

So, total number of identical prisms needed $=6 \times 2=12$

According to Gauss's law, $\Phi_{\text {total }}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\epsilon_0}$

By symmetry, each of the 12 identical prisms receives an equal share of the total flux.

\Phi_{\text {prism }}=\frac{\Phi_{\text {total }}}{12}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{12 \epsilon_0}

question: An infinite, uniformly charged sheet with surface charge density $\sigma$ cuts through a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $R$ at a distance $x$ from its centre, as shown in the figure. The electric flux through the Gaussian surface is
solution:
According to Gauss's Law, the total electric flux $\Phi$ passing through any closed surface is proportional to the total net charge enclosed within that surface, $\Phi=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0}$

The spherical Gaussian surface has a radius R.

An infinite sheet of charge cuts across the sphere at a perpendicular distance x from the centre of the sphere.

The intersection of a plane and a sphere is a planar circle. Therefore, the portion of the charged sheet enclosed inside the spherical Gaussian surface forms a circular disk.

Let $\mathrm{r}_{\text {disk }}$ be the radius of this circular cross-section.

By the Pythagorean theorem $\mathrm{x}^2+\mathrm{r}_{\text {disk }}^2=\mathrm{R}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}_{\text {disk }}^2=\mathrm{R}^2-\mathrm{x}^2$

The area A of this circular disk inside the sphere is $\mathrm{A}=\pi \mathrm{r}_{\text {disk }}^2=\pi\left(\mathrm{R}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right)$

\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}=\sigma \cdot \mathrm{A}=\pi\left(\mathrm{R}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right) \sigma

\Phi=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0}=\frac{\pi\left(\mathrm{R}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right) \sigma}{\epsilon_0}

Thus, the correct option is (D).

question: A point charge $q$ is placed at the centre of left circular end of a cylinder of length $l = 4\ \text{cm}$ and radius $R = 3\ \text{cm}$ as shown. Then, the electric flux through the curved surface of the cylinder is
solution:
Let a point charge $q$ be placed at the origin. Consider a circular disk of radius $R$ located at a perpendicular distance d from the charge along its central axis.

The electric field produced by the point charge at a distance r is $\mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{r}^2}$

To find the flux through the disk, let a thin ring of radius y and width dy on the disk.

Distance from the charge to this ring $\mathrm{r}=\sqrt{\mathrm{d}^2+\mathrm{y}^2}$

The area of this elemental ring is $\mathrm{dA}=2 \pi \mathrm{y} \mathrm{dy}$

The normal vector to the disk is along the axis. The angle $\theta$ between the electric field and the normal to the disk is,

$\cos\theta = \frac{d}{r} = \frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2 + y^2}}$

The electric flux through this differential ring is

d\Phi = E\cos\theta\,dA = \left(\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(d^2+y^2)}\right)\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2+y^2}}\right)(2\pi y\,dy)

d\Phi = \frac{qd}{2\varepsilon_0}\frac{y\,dy}{(d^2+y^2)^{3/2}}

Total flux is the sum from $0$ to $R$ is,

\Phi_{\text{disk}} = \frac{qd}{2\varepsilon_0}\int\limits_{0}^{R} \frac{y}{(d^2+y^2)^{3/2}}\,dy

Let $u = d^2 + y^2$, so $du = 2y\,dy$,

\Phi_{\text{disk}} = \frac{qd}{2\varepsilon_0}\left[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{d^2+y^2}}\right]_{0}^{R} = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2+R^2}}\right)

The semi-vertical angle $\alpha$ subtended by the rim of the disk at the charge $\left(\cos\alpha = \frac{d}{\sqrt{d^2+R^2}}\right)$.

\Phi_{\text{disk}} = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}(1-\cos\alpha)

The point charge $q$ is at its centre $(d \Rightarrow 0)$. Electric field lines emerging from the charge into the interior of the cylinder lie parallel to the planar surface of this base $\Phi_{\text{left face}} = 0$

The right circular disk of radius $R = 3\ \text{cm}$ located at distance $l = 4\ \text{cm}$ from the charge.

A point charge q radiates a total flux of $\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$ uniformly into all directions $(4\pi$ steradians$)$.

Because the charge is at the flat boundary of the left face, half of the total flux enters the interior half-space containing the cylinder.

\Phi_{\text{interior}} = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}

The flux through the right circular face $(\Phi_{\text{right}})$ using the derived formula for the disk with distance $d = l = 4\ \text{cm}$ and radius $R = 3\ \text{cm}$.

\cos \alpha = \frac{l}{\sqrt{l^2 + R^2}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{16 + 9}} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{4}{5}

Therefore, the flux passing through the right circular base is

\Phi_{\text{right}} = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}(1 - \cos \alpha) = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{4}{5}\right) = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{q}{10\varepsilon_0}

All flux entering the interior of the cylinder must exit through either the curved surface or the right circular face.

\Phi_{\text{interior}} = \Phi_{\text{curved}} + \Phi_{\text{right}}

\Phi_{\text{curved}} = \Phi_{\text{interior}} - \Phi_{\text{right}}

\Phi_{\text{curved}} = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_0} - \frac{q}{10\varepsilon_0} = \frac{5q}{10\varepsilon_0} - \frac{q}{10\varepsilon_0} = \frac{4q}{10\varepsilon_0} = \frac{2q}{5\varepsilon_0}

Thus, the correct option is (B)

question: A positively charged pendulum is oscillating in a uniform electric field as shown in Figure. Its time period of SHM as compared to that when it was uncharged. (mg > qE)
solution:
For a simple pendulum of length l and bob mass m, the restoring torque when displaced by a small angle $\theta$ from the vertical is due to gravity only.

\tau = -(mg\sin\theta)\cdot l \approx -mgl\theta

Using the equation of rotational motion $\tau = I\alpha$

Here, $I$ is the moment of inertia of bob about point of suspension and $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration caused.

\Rightarrow \frac{I\mathrm{d}^2\theta}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = -mgl\theta

Since the moment of inertia about the hinge is $I = ml^2$,

ml^2\frac{\mathrm{d}^2\theta}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = -mgl\theta \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d}^2\theta}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = -\left(\frac{g}{l}\right)\theta

For rotational simple harmonic motion, $\alpha = -\omega^2\theta$.

Thus, the angular frequency is $\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{g}}{1}}$, and the time period when uncharged is,

\mathrm{T}_0=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{~g}}}

When uniform electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is directed vertically upwards.

Since the bob has a positive charge +q, the electrostatic force is in the direction of the electric field (vertically upwards).

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{e}}=+\mathrm{qE} \hat{\mathrm{~J}}

The downward gravitational force is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{g}}=-\mathrm{mg} \hat{\jmath}$

The net downward force acting along the vertical line in equilibrium is $\mathrm{F}_{\text {net }}=\mathrm{mg}-\mathrm{qE}$

Since it is given that $\mathrm{mg}>\mathrm{qE}$, the net downward force remains positive, which means the equilibrium (mean) position is still the lowest point with the string vertically downward.

The effective acceleration due to the combined downward forces is,

\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{net}}}{\mathrm{~m}}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}-\mathrm{qE}}{\mathrm{~m}}=\mathrm{g}-\frac{\mathrm{qE}}{\mathrm{~m}}

Since $\mathrm{q}>0, \mathrm{E}>0$, and $\mathrm{m}>0 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{qE}}{\mathrm{m}}>0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~g}_{\text {eff }}<\mathrm{g}$

When the pendulum is displaced by a small angle $\theta$ from the vertical, the restoring force directed towards the mean position is

F_{\text{restoring}} = -(mg - qE)\sin\theta = -m g_{\text{eff}}\sin\theta

For small angles, $\sin\theta \approx \theta \Rightarrow \tau = -(m g_{\text{eff}}\theta)l$

Using $\tau = I\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = ml^2\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}$,

ml^2\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -m g_{\text{eff}} l\theta \Rightarrow \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\left(\frac{g_{\text{eff}}}{l}\right)\theta

So, the new time period $T$ is,

T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g - \frac{qE}{m}}}

Because $g_{\text{eff}} = g - \frac{qE}{m} < g$, the denominator $g - \frac{qE}{m} < g$ (decreases).

As the denominator decreases, the value of the fraction $\frac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}$ increases.

\frac{l}{g - \frac{qE}{m}} > \frac{l}{g} \Rightarrow T > T_0

Therefore, the time period of oscillation will increase. Thus, the correct option is (A).

question: The particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ will touch the infinitely large plate of uniform charge density $\sigma$ if its velocity $v$ is more than : (Given that $\sigma q > 0$)
solution:
Let a large flat sheet carrying a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$.

By Gauss's law, the electric field is perpendicular to the plate everywhere, pointing outwards on both sides with a magnitude of $\mathrm{E}=\frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0}$

We are given that $\sigma \mathrm{q}>0$, which means both the plate and the particle have the same sign of charge, either both are positive or both are negative. So, the plate repels the particle.

The electrostatic repulsive force acting on the particle is F = qE = q\frac{\rho}{2\theta_0} = \frac{\rho q}{2\theta_0}

By Newton's second law ($F = ma$), the retarding acceleration opposing the motion towards the plate is

a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{\rho q}{2m\theta_0}

Let the particle be projected towards the plate from an initial distance $d$ with initial speed $v$.

Since the acceleration is constant, so we can use kinematic equation.

To just reach (touch) the plate, its velocity must be greater than zero when it reaches the plate, meaning the critical minimum velocity $v_{\min}$ is the speed at which its final velocity $v_f$ becomes zero right at the surface of the plate ($x = d$).

Using the third equation of motion:

v_f^2 = v_i^2 - 2a(\triangle x)

0 = v_{\min}^2 - 2\bigg(\frac{\rho q}{2m\theta_0}\bigg)d

v_{\min}^2 = \frac{\rho q d}{m\theta_0}

v_{\min} = \frac{\rho q d}{m\theta_0}

For the particle to successfully touch the plate, its initial velocity $v$ must be greater than this critical value,

v > \frac{\rho q d}{m\theta_0}

Thus, the correct option is (C).

question: The linear charge density on upper half of semi-circular section of ring is $\lambda$ and that at lower half is $-\lambda$. The direction of electric field at centre O of ring is :
solution:
Let the centre O of the semi-circular arc be the origin $(0,0)$.

The semi-circular section of radius $R$ extending from $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$ through $\theta=\pi$ to $\theta=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$.

The upper half has a positive linear charge density $+\lambda$ (from angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $\pi$ ).

The lower half has a negative linear charge density $-\lambda$ (from angle $\pi$ to $\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ ).

The arc length of this element is $\mathrm{ds}=\mathrm{R} \mathrm{d} \theta$

The charge on this small element is $\mathrm{dq}=\lambda(\theta) \mathrm{ds}=\lambda(\theta) \mathrm{R} \mathrm{d} \theta$

The magnitude of the electric field produced at the origin O by this charge element is given by Coulomb's law,

\mathrm{dE}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{|\mathrm{dq}|}{\mathrm{R}^2}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{|\lambda(\theta)| \mathrm{Rd} \theta}{\mathrm{R}^2}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{|\lambda(\theta)| \mathrm{d} \theta}{\mathrm{R}}

The position vector of the element on the ring is

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}=\mathrm{R} \cos \theta \hat{\imath}+\mathrm{R} \sin \theta \hat{\jmath}

The electric field at the origin due to a charge dq is directed along $-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}$ for a positive charge and along $+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}$ for a negative charge.

\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{\mathrm{dq}}{\mathrm{R}^2} \hat{\mathrm{r}}^{\prime}=-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{R}^2} \mathrm{dq}(\cos \theta \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\sin \theta \hat{\mathrm{\jmath}})

Substituting $\mathrm{dq}=\lambda(\theta) \mathrm{Rd} \theta$,

d \vec{E}=-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R} \lambda(\theta)(\cos \theta \hat{\imath}+\sin \theta \hat{\jmath}) d \theta

The upper half extends from $\theta \in\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]$, where $\lambda(\theta)=+\lambda$

The lower half extends from $\theta \in\left[\pi, \frac{3 \pi}{2}\right]$, where $\lambda(\theta)=-\lambda$

E_x=-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}\left[(0-1)-(-1-0)\right]

E_x=-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}\left[(-1)-(-1)\right]=-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}[0]=0

The horizontal components from the upper and lower halves cancels each other out.

E_y=-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}\left[\left((-\cos(\pi))-(-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right))\right)-\left((-\cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right))-(-\cos(\pi))\right)\right]

E_y=-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}\left[1-(-1)\right]=-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}[2]=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}

question: A charge Q is placed at each of opposite corners of a square. A charge q is placed at each of the other two corners. If the net electrical force on Q is zero, then $\frac{Q}{q}$ equals
solution:
Let the four corners of the square of side length a be A, B, C and D.

Corners A and C are opposite corners, each holding a charge Q.

Corners B and D are the other two opposite corners, each holding a charge q.

The distances from corner A to the corner B and D are $r_{AB}=a, r_{AD}=a$

Using Pythagoras theorem, the distances from corner A to the corner C is;

r_{AC}=\sqrt{a^2+a^2}=a\sqrt{2}

Using Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force between two point charges $q_i$ and $q_j$ separated by a distance r is

\vec{F}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_iq_j}{r^2}\hat{r}

The net force $\vec{F}_{\mathrm{net}}$ on charge Q at corner A is the vector sum of the forces exerted by the other three charges.

\vec{F}_{\mathrm{net}}=\vec{F}_{12}+\vec{F}_{14}+\vec{F}_{13}

Let for Cartesian coordinate system the origin $(0,0)$ at corner A.

Force exerted on Q at $(0,0)$ by charge q at $(a,0)$ is,

\vec{F}_{12}=-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qq}{a^2}\hat{i}

Force exerted on Q at $(0,0)$ by charge q at $(0,a)$ is

\vec{F}_{14}=-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qq}{a^2}\hat{j}

The resultant of these two mutually perpendicular forces is

\vec{F}_{12}+\vec{F}_{14}=-\frac{\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}Qq}{a^2}(\hat{i}+\hat{j})

Magnitude of this resultant vector is

\left|\vec{F}_{12}+\vec{F}_{14}\right|=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qq}{a^2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qq}{a^2}\right)^2}=\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qq}{a^2}\right)

This resultant acts along the diagonal line joining $(0,0)$ and $(a,a)$.

Distance between the two opposite corners is $r_{13}=a\sqrt{2}$.

The force exerted by Q at $(a,a)$ on Q at $(0,0)$ acts along the diagonal.

\vec{F}_{13}=-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q^2}{(a\sqrt{2})^2}\left(\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=-\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q^2}{2a^2}\frac{(\hat{i}+\hat{j})}{\sqrt{2}}

So, the magnitude of this diagonal force is $F_{13}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q^2}{2a^2}$

For the net force $\vec{F}_{\mathrm{net}}$ to become zero,

\Rightarrow \frac{Q}{2}=-\sqrt{2}q \Rightarrow \frac{Q}{q}=-2\sqrt{2}

Thus, the correct option is (B).

question:
Two small spherical balls each carrying a charge $Q = 10 \mu \text{C}$ are suspended by two insulating threads of equal lengths 1 m each, from a point fixed in the ceiling. It is found that in equilibrium threads are separated by an angle $60^\circ$ between them, as shown in the figure. What is the tension in the threads?

(Given, $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{Nm}^2/\text{C}^2$)
solution:
Let the point of suspension on the ceiling be O .

The two identical balls are suspended by light insulating threads of equal length, $\mathrm{L}=1 \mathrm{~m}$

In equilibrium, the angle between the two threads is $2 \theta=60^{\circ}$.

By symmetry, each thread makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical, $\theta=\frac{60^{\circ}}{2}=30^{\circ}$

The horizontal separation r between the two balls

Triangle OAB formed by the suspension point O and the two balls A and B is an isosceles triangle with two equal sides of length $\mathrm{L}=1 \mathrm{~m}$.

Since the apex angle is $60^{\circ}$, the remaining two base angles must also be equal.

\alpha=\frac{180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}}{2}=60^{\circ}

Hence, triangle OAB is an equilateral triangle, the separation between the charges is equal to the length of the string $r = L = 1 \text{ m}$

For each ball tension $(T)$ acts along the thread, directed toward the suspension point O at an angle $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ with the vertical.

Electrostatic repulsive force $(F_e)$ acts horizontally away from the other positively charged ball.

Gravitational force $(mg)$ acts vertically downwards.

Using Coulomb's law for the electrostatic repulsion, the magnitude of the repulsive force between two charges Q separated by distance r is:

F_e = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q^2}{r^2}

Substituting the given values $(Q = 10\mu C = 10^{-5} \text{ C}, r = 1 \text{ m}, \text{ and } \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{C}^2)$,

F_e = \frac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (10^{-5})^2}{(1)^2}

F_e = \frac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (10^{-10})}{1} = 9 \times 10^{-1} = 0.9 \text{ N}

The horizontal component of the string tension balances the horizontal electrostatic force

T \sin \theta = F_e \Rightarrow T \sin 30^{\circ} = 0.9 \text{ N}

T \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 0.9 \text{ N}

T = 2 \times 0.9 \text{ N} = 1.8 \text{ N}

Thus, the correct option is (B)

question: A small spherical conductor A of radius $a$ is initially charged to a potential $V$ and then placed inside an uncharged spherical conducting shell B of radius $6a$ as shown in figure. The potential of the spherical conductor A after closing the switch S is
solution:
Spherical conductor A has radius $r_A=a$.

It is initially charged to an electric potential $V$.

The initial potential of an isolated spherical conductor of radius a carrying charge $Q$ is $V=\frac{k Q}{a} \Rightarrow Q=\frac{V a}{k}$, where $k=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0}$.

Conductor A is placed inside an uncharged, concentric spherical conducting shell B of radius $r_B=6 a$.

Shell B has initial charge $Q_B=0$.

A switch $S$ connects the inner sphere A directly to the outer shell B.

When the switch S is closed, a conducting path is established between the inner conductor A and the outer shell B. Charges are free to flow until the potential of both conductors becomes equal, $\boldsymbol{V}_{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{V}_{\boldsymbol{B}}^{\prime}$

In any conductor or system of connected conductors, like charges repel each other to the outermost possible boundary to minimize electrostatic potential energy.

For any closed Gaussian surface within the material of shell B enclosing the cavity, the electric field must become zero $\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{E}}=\overrightarrow{\mathbf{0}}$.

By Gauss's law, the net enclosed charge inside shell B must become zero $\boldsymbol{q}_{\text {enclosed }}=\boldsymbol{Q}_{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}$

Consequently, the charge Q completely transfers from the inner conductor A to the outer surface of shell B.

Q_A^{\prime}=0, Q_B^{\prime}=Q

After the charge transfer, all the charge Q resides uniformly on the outer surface of shell B of radius $6 \boldsymbol{a}$.

The electric field inside the hollow shell $\mathrm{B}(\boldsymbol{r}<\mathbf{6 a})$ is zero everywhere, $\overrightarrow{\boldsymbol{E}}=\overrightarrow{\mathbf{0}}$ for $\boldsymbol{r}<\mathbf{6 a}$

Since the electric field inside shell B is zero, the electrostatic potential is uniform throughout from the centre to its outer surface, $\boldsymbol{V}(\boldsymbol{r})=\boldsymbol{V}_{\text {shell }}=\frac{\boldsymbol{k} \boldsymbol{Q}}{\boldsymbol{r}_{\boldsymbol{B}}}$ for all $\boldsymbol{r} \leq \boldsymbol{r}_{\boldsymbol{B}}$

Therefore, the potential of conductor A (which lies inside shell B ) is $\boldsymbol{V}_{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}=\frac{\boldsymbol{k} \boldsymbol{Q}}{\mathbf{6} \boldsymbol{a}}$

Substituting $\boldsymbol{V}=\frac{\boldsymbol{k} \boldsymbol{Q}}{\boldsymbol{a}}, \boldsymbol{V}_{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathbf{1}}{\mathbf{6}}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{k} \boldsymbol{Q}}{\boldsymbol{a}}\right)=\frac{\boldsymbol{V}}{\mathbf{6}}$

Thus, the correct option is (D).

question: Shown in figure are two uniformly charged spherical thin shells. Total electric potential energy of the system will be
solution:
An inner thin spherical shell of radius $\mathrm{R}_1=\mathrm{R}$ carrying a uniform charge $\mathrm{q}_1=+\mathrm{Q}$.

An outer thin spherical shell of radius $\mathrm{R}_2=3 \mathrm{R}$ carrying a uniform charge $\mathrm{q}_2=-\mathrm{Q}$.

The shells are concentric, with their common centre at the origin $(0,0)$.

Consider assembling a thin spherical shell of radius R by bringing infinitesimal charge elements dq from infinity to the surface of the shell.

When the accumulated charge on the shell is $q$, the electric potential at its surface is V = \frac{kq}{R}

The work done in bringing an additional infinitesimal charge $dq'$ from infinity to the surface of the shell against the electrostatic repulsion is dW = V\,dq = \frac{kq}{R}\,dq

So, total work done to charge the spherical shell with charge $q$ is stored as self-energy of charged shell.

U_{\text{self}} = \int\limits_{0}^{q} \frac{kq}{R}\,dq = \frac{k}{R}\left[\frac{q^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{q} = \frac{kq^2}{2R}

Self-energy of the inner shell (radius $R$, charge $+Q$), U_1 = \frac{k(+Q)^2}{2R} = \frac{kQ^2}{2R}

Self-energy of the inner shell (radius $3R$, charge $-Q$), U_2 = \frac{k(-Q)^2}{2\cdot 3R} = \frac{kQ^2}{6R}

The interaction energy $U_{12}$ between two charge distributions is the work done to bring the charge of one shell from infinity into the electric potential field produced by the other shell.

The electric potential produced by the outer shell of radius $3R$ and charge $-Q$ at any point inside it $(r < R)$ is constant.

V_2(\text{inside}) = \frac{kq_2}{R_2} = \frac{k(-Q)}{3R} = -\frac{kQ}{3R}

Since every point on the inner shell of radius $R$ lies inside the outer shell, the potential produced by the outer shell everywhere on the inner shell is constant, V_2(\text{inside}) = -\frac{kQ}{3R}

The interaction energy is the product of the charge of the inner shell $q_1 = +Q$ and the potential due to the inner shell at that radius, U_{12} = q_1 \cdot V_1(\text{inside}) = (+Q) \times \left(-\frac{kQ}{3R}\right) = -\frac{kQ^2}{3R}

The total potential energy $U$ of the system is the sum of the self-energies and the interaction energy,

U = U_1 + U_2 + U_{12}

U = \frac{kQ^2}{2R} + \frac{kQ^2}{6R} - \frac{kQ^2}{3R}

U = \frac{kQ^2}{R}\left(\frac{3}{6} + \frac{1}{6} - \frac{2}{6}\right)

U = \frac{kQ^2}{R}\left(\frac{3 + 1 - 2}{6}\right) = \frac{kQ^2}{R}\left(\frac{2}{6}\right) = \frac{kQ^2}{3R}

Thus, the correct option is (D)

question: A point charge placed on the axis of an uniformly charged disc experiences a force F due to the disc. If the charge density on the disc is $\sigma$, the electric flux through the disc, due to the point charge will be
solution:
Let a circular disk of radius R lying in the $\mathrm{y}-\mathrm{z}$ plane with uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. And a point P lie on its central axis (x-axis) at a distance x from the centre of the disk.

The disk can be broken down into concentric rings of radius r and radial width dr .

Area of the ring is $\mathrm{dA}=2 \pi \mathrm{r} \mathrm{dr}$

Charge on the ring is $dq = \sigma\, dA = 2\pi\sigma r\,dr$

Distance from any point on the ring to point P is $s = \sqrt{x^2 + r^2}$

By symmetry, components of the electric field perpendicular to the axis cancel out.

The axial component of electric field is $dE = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{dq}{s^2}\cos\theta$, where $\cos\theta = \frac{x}{s} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + r^2}}$.

Substituting $dq$ and $\cos\theta$:

dE = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2\pi\sigma r\,dr}{x^2 + r^2}\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + r^2}}\right) = \frac{\sigma x}{2\epsilon_0}\frac{r\,dr}{(x^2 + r^2)^{3/2}}

The net electric field is the vector sum of all elemental rings taken from $r = 0$ to $r = R$.

E = \frac{\sigma x}{2\epsilon_0}\int\limits_{0}^{R} \frac{r\,dr}{(x^2 + r^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{\sigma x}{2\epsilon_0}\left[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + r^2}}\right]_{0}^{R}

E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)

Let the point charge placed at P be $q$. The force $F$ experienced by the charge $q$ due to the electric field of the disk is

F = qE = \frac{q\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left(1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)

The solid angle $\Omega$ subtended by a circular disk of radius R at a point on its axis at distance x is $\Omega = 2\pi \left(1 - \cos \theta_0\right)$, where $\cos \theta_0 = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}$.

Thus

\Omega = 2\pi \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)

Since a point charge q radiates an electric flux of $\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$ into the full solid angle of $4\pi$ steradians, the flux passing through the solid angle $\Omega$ is:

\Phi = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \left(\dfrac{\Omega}{4\pi}\right) = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \left[\dfrac{2\pi \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)}{4\pi}\right] = \dfrac{q}{2\varepsilon_0} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)

Putting

\Phi = \dfrac{q}{2\varepsilon_0} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)

in the expression for force,

F = \sigma \left[\dfrac{q}{2\varepsilon_0} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + R^2}}\right)\right]

F = \sigma \cdot \Phi \Rightarrow \Phi = \dfrac{F}{\sigma}

Thus, the correct option is (D).

question: Two short electric dipoles are placed as shown in figure. The energy of electric interaction between these dipoles will be
solution:
The potential energy $U$ of an electric dipole of moment $\vec{P}_1$ placed in an external electric field $\vec{E}_2$ produced by another dipole $\vec{P}_2$ is the work done by an external torque to rotate the dipole into position.

\mathrm{U}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_1 \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2

Dipole $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_2$ is at the origin and is horizontally to the right along the positive horizontal axis.

Dipole $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_1$ is at a distance r from $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_2$, along a line that makes an angle $\theta$ with the axis of dipole $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_2$.

Let the unit vector along the line joining the two dipoles is $\hat{\mathrm{r}}, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_1=\mathrm{p}_1 \widehat{\mathrm{r}}$

We can resolve dipole $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_2$ into two perpendicular components,

Component along the radial line $\mathrm{p}_{2| |}=\mathrm{p}_2 \cos \theta$

Component perpendicular to the radial line is $\mathrm{p}_{2 \perp}=\mathrm{p}_2 \sin \theta$

The radial component $\mathrm{p}_{2 \|}=\mathrm{p}_2 \cos \theta$ acts as an axial dipole for point $(\mathrm{r}, \theta)$. The electric field along the axis of a short dipole is directed along the dipole moment and has magnitude $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{k}\left(\mathrm{p}_2 \cos \theta\right)}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

The transverse component $\mathrm{p}_{2 \perp}=\mathrm{p}_2 \sin \theta$ acts as an equatorial dipole for point $(\mathrm{r}, \theta)$. The equatorial electric field is directed antiparallel to the dipole component and has magnitude, $\mathrm{E}_\theta=\frac{\mathrm{k}\left(\mathrm{p}_2 \sin \theta\right)}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

The total electric field vector produced by dipole $\vec{P}_2$ at the location of dipole $\vec{P}_1$ is

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{r}} \hat{\mathrm{r}}+\mathrm{E}_\theta \hat{\theta}=\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{kp}_2 \cos \theta}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right) \hat{\mathrm{r}}+\left(\frac{\mathrm{kp}_2 \sin \theta}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right) \hat{\theta}

Substituting $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_1=\mathrm{p}_1 \widehat{\mathrm{r}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2$ into the energy formula,

\mathrm{U}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_1 \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=-\left(\mathrm{p}_1 \hat{\mathrm{r}}\right) \cdot\left[\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{kp}_2 \cos \theta}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right) \hat{\mathrm{r}}+\left(\frac{\mathrm{kp}_2 \sin \theta}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right) \hat{\theta}\right]

Since $\hat{\mathrm{r}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{r}}=1$ and $\hat{\mathrm{r}} \cdot \hat{\theta}=0$,

\mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{p}_1\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{kp}_2 \cos \theta}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right)=-\frac{2 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{p}_1 \mathrm{p}_2 \cos \theta}{\mathrm{r}^3}

Thus, the correct option is (B).

infinity).

The number of lines originating from a positive charge +q or terminating on a negative charge -q is directly proportional to the magnitude of the charge $|\mathrm{q}|$.

A charge distribution that is symmetric must create an electric field lines symmetrical.

In a region between like charges, there can exist neutral points where the net electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\overrightarrow{0}$. At such points, no field lines can pass through, so lines bending away from each other.

Left charge at $\mathrm{x}=-\mathrm{a}$ is charge is -Q .

question: Which of the following represents the equipotential lines of a dipole (two equal and opposite charges placed at small separation)?
solution:
Let an electric dipole consisting of charge +q at $\left(0, \frac{\mathrm{~d}}{2}\right)$ and charge -q at $\left(0,-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}\right)$ on the y -axis.

The potential at any arbitrary point $(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})$ is the superposition of the potentials due to individual charges.

\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{r}_{+}}-\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{r}_{-}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{x}^2+\left(\mathrm{y}-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}\right)^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{x}^2+\left(\mathrm{y}+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}\right)^2}}\right)

For an equipotential line the electric potential $\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})$ is constant at every point.

\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})=\text { constant }=\mathrm{C} .

At any point on the perpendicular bisector (the x -axis, where $\mathrm{y}=0$ ) the distances from the charges are,

r_{+}=\sqrt{x^2+\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2}=r_{-}

So, electric potential at this point is $\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, 0)=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_{+}}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{r}_{+}}\right)=0$

Therefore, the straight perpendicular line bisecting the segment joining the two charges is an equipotential line corresponding to $\mathrm{V}=0$.

Very close to the positive charge +q , its own potential dominates, and the influence of -q is nearly constant

\mathrm{V} \approx \frac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{r}_{+}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}_{+} \approx \text { constant }

Thus, near +q, the equipotential lines are closed curves (nearly circular) surrounding +q with positive potential (V > 0).

Similarly, near -q , the equipotential lines are closed curves surrounding -q with negative potential $(\mathrm{V}<0)$.

Equipotential lines are always mutually perpendicular to the electric field lines $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=-\nabla \mathrm{V})$.

Because the electric field lines originate on +q , curve outward, and terminate on -q , the equipotential lines enclose each charge separately; they do not cross each other.

Thus, the correct option is (D).

solution:

The displacement vector pointing from $-q$ to $+q$ is $\vec{d}=\vec{r}_{+}-\vec{r}_{-}$.

Therefore, the dipole moment vector is :

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{q} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~d}}=\mathrm{q}\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{+}-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{-}\right)

Using the principle of superposition, the resultant (net) dipole moment of the entire system is the vector sum of the individual dipole moments :

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_{\mathrm{net}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_1+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_2+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_3 \ldots=\sum \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_{\mathrm{i}}

Charge $+q$ is at ( $0, a, 0$ ). Position vector is $\vec{r}_1=a \hat{j}$

Charge $-2 q$ is at $(0,0,0)$ (the origin). Position vector is $\vec{r}_2=0 \hat{\imath}+0 \hat{\jmath}=\overrightarrow{0}$

Charge $+q$ is at ( $a, 0,0$ ). Position vector is $\vec{r}_3=$ aî

The displacement vector points from origin to $(a, 0,0)$ is $\vec{d}_1=a \hat{i}-\overrightarrow{0}=a \hat{i}$

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_1=\mathrm{q} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~d}}_1=\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{a} \hat{\mathrm{i}})=\mathrm{qa} \hat{\mathrm{i}}

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_2=\mathrm{q} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~d}}_2=\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{a} \hat{\jmath})=\mathrm{qa} \hat{\jmath}

question: Electric field intensity at point $P$ due to below configuration for $r \gg a$ is given by $n \times \frac{k p a}{r^m}$, where $p=$ qa. Find the value of $\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{n}$.
solution:
Along a straight vertical line, three charges are arranged symmetrically.

A charge +q at $\mathrm{y}=+\mathrm{a}$, second charge -2 q at the origin $\mathrm{y}=0$, and the third +q at $\mathrm{y}=-\mathrm{a}$

The observation point P lies on the along the x -axis (axis of dipole) at a distance r from the origin, such that $\mathrm{r} \gg$ a.

By the principle of superposition, the net electric field at P is

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_1+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_3

The electric field due to the charge -2 q at the origin points towards the origin.

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=-\frac{\mathrm{k}(2 \mathrm{q})}{\mathrm{r}^2} \hat{\imath}

The distance from each charge $+q$ to point P is $d_1 = r + a$ and $d_3 = r - a$

The magnitude of the field from $q_1 = +q$ is $E_1 = \dfrac{kq_1}{d_1^2} = \dfrac{kq}{(r+a)^2}$ (towards right)

The magnitude of the field from $q_2 = +q$ is $E_3 = \dfrac{kq_3}{d_3^2} = \dfrac{kq}{(r-a)^2}$ (towards right)

The net electric field at point P is;

\vec{E} = \vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2 + \vec{E}_3 = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + \left[\dfrac{kq}{(r+a)^2}\hat{i}\right] + \left[\dfrac{kq}{(r-a)^2}\hat{i}\right]

\vec{E} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + kq\left[\dfrac{1}{(r-a)^2} + \dfrac{1}{(r+a)^2}\right]

\vec{E} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + kq\left[\dfrac{(r+a)^2 + (r-a)^2}{(r^2-a^2)^2}\right] = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + kq\left[\dfrac{2(r^2+a^2)}{(r^2-a^2)^2}\right]\hat{i}

\vec{E} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + kq\left[\dfrac{2r^2\left(1+\dfrac{a^2}{r^2}\right)}{r^4\left(1-\dfrac{a^2}{r^2}\right)^2}\right]\hat{i} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + \dfrac{2kq}{r^2}\left[\left(1+\dfrac{a^2}{r^2}\right)\left(1-\dfrac{a^2}{r^2}\right)^{-2}\right]\hat{i}

\vec{E} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + \dfrac{2kq}{r^2}\left[\left(1+\dfrac{a^2}{r^2}\right)\left(1+\dfrac{2a^2}{r^2}\right)\right]\hat{i} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + \dfrac{2kq}{r^2}\left(1+\dfrac{2a^2}{r^2}+\dfrac{a^2}{r^2}+\dfrac{2a^4}{r^4}\right)\hat{i}

\vec{E} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + \dfrac{2kq}{r^2}\left(1+\dfrac{3a^2}{r^2}\right)\hat{i} = \left[-\dfrac{k(2q)}{r^2}\hat{i}\right] + \left(\dfrac{2kq}{r^2}+\dfrac{6kqa^2}{r^4}\right)\hat{i}

|\vec{E}| = \dfrac{6kqa^2}{r^4} = \dfrac{6k(qa)a}{r^4} = \dfrac{6kpa}{r^4} = n \times \dfrac{kpa}{r^m}

\Rightarrow n = 6, m = 4 \Rightarrow m + n = 10

Therefore, the value of $m + n$ is 10.

question: An infinitely long solid cylinder of radius $R$ has a uniform charge density $\rho$. It has a spherical cavity of radius $\frac{R}{2}$ with its centre on the axis of the cylinder(as shown in figure). The magnitude of the electric field at point $P$, which is at a distance $2 R$ from the axis of the cylinder, is given by $\frac{23 \rho R}{6 K \epsilon_0}$. The value of $K$ is
solution:
The charged cylinder with a cavity can be assumed as a complete solid cylinder of radius R with a spherical cavity of radius $\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2}$.

Let the uniform volume charge density of solid cylinder is $+\rho$ then for cavity uniform volume charge density is $-\rho$.

The net electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\text {net }}$ at point P is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\text {net }}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\text {cylinder }}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\text {cavity }}$

The cavity is spherical of radius $\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2}$ and located at the axis of cylinder.

Point P is located at a distance $\mathrm{r}=2 \mathrm{R}$ from the axis of the cylinder.

Let a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $\mathrm{r}=2 \mathrm{R}$ and length L .

By cylindrical symmetry, the electric field is directed radially outward from the axis.

\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{a} = E_{\mathrm{cyl}} \cdot (2\pi r L) = E_{\mathrm{cyl}} \cdot (2\pi (2R) L) = 4\pi R L\, E_{\mathrm{cyl}}

The total charge enclosed by this Gaussian surface of radius $2R$ is the charge of the cylinder of radius $R$

q_{\mathrm{enclosed}} = \rho \cdot (\pi R^2 L)

Applying Gauss's law

E_{\mathrm{cyl}} \cdot (4\pi R L) = \frac{\rho\pi R^2 L}{\epsilon_0} \Rightarrow E_{\mathrm{cyl}} = \frac{\rho R}{4\epsilon_0}

This field is directed away from the cylinder's axis, radially outwards along the line to P.

The spherical cavity of radius $\frac{R}{2}$ is placed at the axis of of the cylinder, so the centre of this sphere is at a distance $r_s = 2R$ from the axis of the cylinder along the line joining the axis to point P.

The spherical cavity carries a negative charge density $-\rho$.

The magnitude of the charge of this sphere is

q_s = \rho \cdot V = \rho \cdot \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^3\right) = \rho \cdot \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi \frac{R^3}{8}\right) = \frac{\rho\pi R^3}{6}

For any point outside a uniformly charged sphere, the electric field is equal to that of a point charge located at its centre, $E_{\mathrm{sphere}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_s}{r_s^2}$

E_{\mathrm{sphere}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{\frac{\rho\pi R^3}{6}}{(2R)^2} = \frac{\rho R}{96\epsilon_0}

Since the charge density of the cavity is negative, this field $\vec{E}_{\mathrm{sphere}}$ is directed toward the centre of the cavity (opposite to the cylinder's outward field).

So, the net electric field at point P is $\vec{E}_{\mathrm{net}} = E_{\mathrm{cyl}} - E_{\mathrm{sphere}}$

E_{\mathrm{net}} = \frac{\rho R}{4\epsilon_0} - \frac{\rho R}{96\epsilon_0} = \frac{\rho R}{\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{96}\right) = \frac{\rho R}{\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{24 - 1}{96}\right) = \frac{23\rho R}{96\epsilon_0}

The net electric field is given as $\frac{23\rho R}{6K\epsilon_0}$. On comparing the terms $6K = 96 \Rightarrow K = 16$

Thus, the correct answer is 16.

solution:
The rod has total mass m uniformly distributed over its length 1 .

The linear charge density varies along the rod as $\lambda(\mathrm{x})=\lambda_0 \mathrm{x}$

A uniform vertical electric field E acts in the region, so that the upward electrostatic force balances the downward gravitational torque.

For the rod to remain in horizontal equilibrium, the net torque acting on the rod about the hinge O must be zero.

\sum \tau_0=0 \Rightarrow \tau_{\text {gravity }}=\tau_{\text {electrostatic }}

Since the mass m of the rod is uniformly distributed, its centre of mass lies at the geometric midpoint.

\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{2}

The total downward gravitational force is $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{mg}$.

The torque exerted by gravity about the hinge O acts in the clockwise direction (negative).

\tau_{\mathrm{g}}=-\mathrm{mg} \cdot \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{cm}}=-\mathrm{mg}\left(\frac{\mathrm{l}}{2}\right)=-\frac{\mathrm{mgl}}{2}

Considering an infinitesimal element of length dx located at a distance x from the hinge O.

question: A non-conducting ring of mass $m$ and radius $R$ is charged as shown in figure. The charged density, i.e. charged per unit length is $\lambda$. It is then placed on a rough non-conducting horizontal surface plane. At time $t=0$, a uniform electric field $E=E_0 \hat{\mathbf{1}}$ is switched on and the ring starts rolling without sliding. The friction force acting on the ring, when it starts moving is $n \lambda R E_0 \hat{\mathbf{l}}$. Find the value of $\mathbf{n}$.
solution:
The ring lies in the vertical xy -plane resting on a rough horizontal surface along the x -axis.

The second quadrant (from $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $\theta=\pi$ ) has a uniform positive linear charge density $+\lambda$.

The fourth quadrant (from $\theta=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ to $\theta=2 \pi$ or $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ to 0 ) has a uniform negative linear charge density $-\lambda$.

Let the angle $\theta$ be measured counterclockwise from the positive horizontal x-axis.

Considering an infinitesimal element $\mathrm{dl}=\mathrm{Rd} \theta:$

A uniform electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{I}}$ is applied horizontally.

The electrostatic force on element $\mathrm{dq}_1$ is $\mathrm{d}_1=\mathrm{dq}_1 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=(+\lambda \mathrm{R} \mathrm{d} \theta) \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\imath}$

The electrostatic force on the opposite element $\mathrm{dq}_2$ is

\vec{\mathrm{d}F}_2 = \mathrm{d}q_2\,\vec{E} = (-\lambda R\,\mathrm{d}\theta)\,E_0\hat{i}

The sum of these two forces is $\vec{\mathrm{d}F}_1 + \vec{\mathrm{d}F}_2 = 0$

Since every positive charge element in the second quadrant has a diametrically opposite equal and opposite negative charge element in the fourth quadrant, the total net electrostatic force on the ring is zero.

\vec{F}_e = \int\limits{} \mathrm{d}\vec{F} = 0

The position vector of element $\mathrm{d}q_1$ relative to the centre is

\vec{r}_1 = R\cos\theta\,\hat{i} + R\sin\theta\,\hat{j}

The torque on element $\mathrm{d}q_1$ about the centre is

\mathrm{d}\vec{\tau}_1 = \vec{r}_1 \times \mathrm{d}\vec{F}_1 = (R\cos\theta\,\hat{i} + R\sin\theta\,\hat{j}) \times (\lambda R E_0\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\hat{i}) = -\lambda R^2 E_0\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\hat{k}

Similarly, for the opposite element $\mathrm{d}q_2$ at $\vec{r}_2 = -\vec{r}_1$,

\mathrm{d}\vec{\tau}_2 = \vec{r}_2 \times \mathrm{d}\vec{F}_2 = (-\vec{r}_1) \times (-\mathrm{d}\vec{F}_1) = \vec{r}_1 \times \mathrm{d}\vec{F}_1 = \mathrm{d}\vec{\tau}_1

The net torque for the pair over $\theta$ from $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\pi$:

\vec{\tau}_c = 2\int\limits_{\pi/2}^{\pi} (-\lambda R^2 E_0\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta)\hat{k} = -2\lambda R^2 E_0[-\cos\theta]_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\hat{k}

\vec{\tau}_c = -2\lambda R^2 E_0\hat{k}

Thus, the magnitude of the electrostatic torque about the centre is $\tau_c = 2\lambda R^2 E_0$ (clockwise)

Let the horizontal friction force acting on the ring at the point of contact with the ground be $\vec{F} = f\hat{i}$.

Using equation of motion for translational motion for the centre of mass

\Sigma F_x = m\,a_{cm} \Rightarrow f = m\,a_{cm}

Using equation of rotational motion about the centre of mass, (taking clockwise as positive) the torque about the centre of mass is provided by the electric torque $\tau_c$ and the friction force $f$

\Sigma\,\tau_{\mathrm{cm}} = \tau_c - fR = I_{\mathrm{cm}}\,\alpha

For a thin ring of mass $m$ and radius $R$, the moment of inertia about its central axis is $I_{\mathrm{cm}} = mR^2$

Therefore $\tau_c - fR = (mR^2)\alpha$

For rolling without slipping from rest $a_{\mathrm{cm}} = R\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{a_{\mathrm{cm}}}{R}$

\Rightarrow \tau_c - fR = (mR^2)\left(\dfrac{a_{\mathrm{cm}}}{R}\right) = mRa_{\mathrm{cm}}

Since $ma_{\mathrm{cm}} = f \Rightarrow \tau_c - fR = fR$

\tau_c = 2fR \Rightarrow f = \dfrac{\tau_c}{2R}

f = \dfrac{2\lambda R^2 E_0}{2R} = \lambda R E_0

Since $f$ is positive, the friction force acts in the positive x-direction, $\vec{F} = \lambda R E_0\hat{i}$

\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{n} \lambda \mathrm{R} \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{l}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=1

Therefore, the value of n is 1 .
